candidateDecisions.label: Mathematics for economics and financial analysis
Mathematics for biological and life sciences

analysis: The closest option builds quantitative foundations through calculus, linear algebra, numerical analysis, probability, programming and statistics. Algorithms and robotics apply discrete methods and kinematics, with linear-system and data-model work. Database Management Systems and AI Ethics replace vision and early reinforcement learning in this option, supporting computational data organisation and accountability after the introductory programming term. This preserves rigorous applied work without implying a complete proof, algebra or topology sequence. The Earth-systems option uses the same core mathematical methods in geochemical, spatial and energy contexts. Earth Observation applies remote sensing and image analysis to environmental data and Energy & Sustainability gives quantitative preparation for renewable-system design. Earth System Science Tools has direct systems and proxy analysis on its description; it follows Sustainability Essentials I, with separate geology later. The Economics option combines calculus, probability, econometrics and modelling with public economics, finance and strategic decisions. Mathematical modelling and optimisation complement, rather than constitute, dedicated financial mathematics. Description-only Advanced Calculus, Econometrics, Database Management Systems, Reinforcement Learning, Earth System Science Tools, Renewable System Design and Earth’s Resources contribute substantially within their described topics. The selected plans are distinct by the course comparisons below. The life sciences and history directions have evidence but were considered after the three stronger feasible choices. Utrecht’s proof, abstract algebra, topology, later proof-based analysis, manifolds, and mathematics research stay visible as separate requirements. Numerical approximation and multivariable calculus are bounded substantive matches. The optional UCR research row is comparison-only.

alignment.rationale: Both provide programming for mathematical problem solving; UCR supplies a general Python foundation rather than mathematics-specific research programming.
Both teach introductory calculus. Utrecht teaches linear algebra alongside it.
Both study graphs and trees. UCR focuses on algorithms and data structures, while Utrecht also develops combinatorial counting and discrete proofs.
Both develop matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations; the external component also continues calculus.
Both use computational approximation for equations and integrals and assess numerical error.
Both model systems with differential equations; UCR concentrates on linear systems, transforms and state-space representations rather than the full ODE/PDE modelling course.
Both establish probability; UCR integrates probability distributions with estimation, inference and simulation.
Both develop multivariable calculus. Utrecht emphasises proofs and theoretical results in analysis.
UCR logic courses develop formal reasoning, but no selected course reproduces a dedicated proof-writing foundation.
UCR calculus does not reproduce a cumulative proof-intensive analysis course.
UCR has no abstract algebra course in groups and rings.
This later course develops proof-based multivariable analysis and prepares for differentiable manifolds.
Utrecht gives ordinary differential equations and their theory a dedicated course.
General projects and research methods do not reproduce the target’s dedicated mathematics laboratory.
These electives count toward Utrecht’s 45 EC profiling space.
Utrecht requires a 15 EC mathematics thesis. UCR’s optional 15 EC research element is separate from the scheduled courses.
The 45 EC profiling space can include an approved minor.
